table.title: The Causal Relationship Between Stereotype Knowledge and Positive Trait Associations
table.research_questions: We propose that individuals exposed to stereotypes about two new groups will exhibit a selective halo effect that favors the advantaged group. Specifically, we anticipate that the conceptual associations with warmth and competence will be weaker for the disadvantaged group (linked to a negative stereotype) compared to the advantaged group (linked to a neutral stereotype).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: Within-subject ANOVA with one factor and two levels (two target groups: advantaged and disadvantaged).
table.randomization:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions during the learning phase, where one fictitious social group (e.g., blue aliens) is disadvantaged, and the other fictitious social group (e.g., green aliens) is advantaged:
Condition 1. Green aliens are advantaged, and blue aliens are disadvantaged.
Condition 2. Green aliens are disadvantaged, and blue aliens are advantaged.
The condition will be randomly assigned to each participant.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Inclusion criteria - U.S. residents; fluent in English; normal or correct-to-normal vision; no known mental health disorders; having a good performance history on Prolific (e.g., approval rate 98% or higher), having at least completed high school. The above criteria will be screened using Prolific's built-in screeners, based on participants' responses to a set of default questions provided on the platform. Participants will be compensated at a rate of £1 for 7 minutes.

Methodology:
Greeble Stimuli. 
Multi-dimensional object stimuli, such as Greebles (Gauthier & Tarr, 1997), will serve as the images of fictious social being, e.g., “aliens”. To make it easier for participants to distinguish between the two groups, we will assign one skin color to one gender and another skin color to the other (e.g., blue and green). The color palette will have an equal spacing between colors corresponds to equal perceptual differences, controlling the perceived variance in the two groups' colors. Stimuli will be randomly assigned to either, say, the green or blue group. 

Learning Phase.
Participants will be informed that they are going to be introduced to two groups of aliens to report on these new species. The task begins with a learning phase in which participants will view images of 36 Greebles paired with unique behaviors. Each pair will be presented once, resulting in a total of 36 trials. Half of the Greebles will be paired with low-capability behaviors (e.g., has difficulty keeping track of their finances), and the other half will be paired with medium-capability behaviors (e.g., eats an apple every day). The assignment of blue and green Greebles to the disadvantaged or advantaged group will be randomized. In each condition, a majority of disadvantaged group members (e.g., 16 out of 18 disadvantaged group Greebles) will be associated with low-capability behaviors, while a majority of advantaged group members (e.g., 16 out of 18 advantaged group Greebles) will be linked to common-capability behaviors. Participants will view the Greeble behaviors in random order at their own pace and will be asked to visualize the alien engaging in the described behavior on each trial.

Attention check (understanding of group categorization): 
To ensure that participants correctly associate specific behaviors with designated groups as intended by the manipulation, we will include four questions in the manipulation check. Participants will be asked to identify which Greeble is most likely to exhibit a specific behavior by choosing from Greeble group options. For example, they might answer the question, "based on what you‘ve learned, which alien group is the individual most likely to belong to for this behavior: Gets confused by the rules of chess?" Participants will receive feedback on their choices, which will reinforce the stereotypical associations with certain "alien" groups.

Conceptual halo effect.
Next, participants will engage in a conceptual trait association task. In this task, they will assess pairwise conceptual associations for both the advantaged and disadvantaged groups. They will answer four questions in total, with two alien groups and two conceptual directions. They will answer questions such as "If this alien is known to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable), how likely are they to be competent (i.e., capable; smart)?" and "If this alien is known to be competent (i.e., capable; smart), how likely are they to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable)?". The question will be presented along with a picture of an alien from the green/blue group. The picture will be randomly selected from a set of images per group. This approach ensures that participants think at the individual level (rather than the group level), and helps to reduce any bias introduced by a specific alien image. Ratings will be given on a scale from 1 (not at all likely) to 9 (very likely), at the participants' own pace, with stimuli presented in random order.

Manipulation check (explicit group stereotypes).
Manipulation check (explicit stereotype assessment): To ensure that participants develop a favorable stereotype for the advantaged group and an unfavorable stereotype for the disadvantaged group, they will answer four stereotype assessment questions, such as "How warm/competent do you think this group of aliens would be?" with a response scale from 1 (not at all) to 9 (very). During these questions, images of specific groups of Greebles will be displayed to help guide their responses.

Lastly, participants will complete a standard demographics survey. At the end of the study, participants will be compensated and debriefed.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 54 participants. We will attempt to recruit up to 60 participants to account for an anticipated exclusion rate of approximately 10%.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size was calculated with the software G*Power, aiming for an alpha level of 0.05 and a power of 95%. We intend to detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25). Lacking previous data to estimate the correlation among repeated measures, we assume a correlation of 0.5, which is the midpoint of the typical range from 0.3 to 0.7. A power analysis for a repeated measures ANOVA with within-subjects factors showed that at least 54 participants are required to detect this effect.
table.manipulated_variables: Participants' stereotype knowledge of two target groups will be manipulated into two levels: high and low. To achieve this, during the learning phase, a majority of disadvantaged group members (e.g., 16 out of 18 disadvantaged group Greebles) will be associated with low-capability behaviors, while a majority of advantaged group members (e.g., 16 out of 18 advantaged group Greebles) will be linked to common-capability behaviors.
table.measured_variables: The conceptual halo effect for the advantaged and disadvantaged groups will be assessed by asking participants questions such as, "If this alien is known to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable), how likely are they to be competent (i.e., capable; smart)?" and "If this alien is known to be competent (i.e., capable; smart), how likely are they to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable)?" Responses will be rated on a scale from 1 to 9, where 1 indicates "not at all likely" and 9 indicates "very likely."
table.statistical_tests: We will conduct within-subjects ANOVAs with one factor and two levels (two target groups: advantaged and disadvantaged) to analyze the results. This analysis will encompass two models: (1) comparing groups based on the likelihood of being competent when known to be warm, and (2) comparing groups based on the likelihood of being warm when known to be competent. Corrections for multiple comparisons will be applied.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<.05 criterion to determine if the ANOVA shows significant differences from the null hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will conduct attention checks and manipulation checks to verify that participants have understood and engaged with the task as intended.

The attention check aims to confirm that during the learning phase, participants have accurately associated specific behaviors with the designated groups, as directed by the manipulation. Participants will receive feedback on their responses, reinforcing the intended stereotypical associations with certain "alien" groups. The manipulation check is designed to ensure that participants form a favorable stereotype for the advantaged group and an unfavorable stereotype for the disadvantaged group.

The exclusion criteria are as follows: (1) participants will be excluded if they incorrectly answer all four attention check questions; (2) we will use the mean warmth and competence ratings from the manipulation check questions as indicators of the overall impression of each group. Participants will be excluded if they form a more positive impression of the disadvantaged group, indicated by a higher mean rating for the disadvantaged group compared to the advantaged group.
table.missing_data_handling: No missing data is anticipated, as the experiment requires participants to provide a response before moving forward.
table.exploratory_analyses: In addition to assessing positive trait associations, we also plan to explore negative trait associations. Participants will be asked questions such as, "If this alien is known to be not warm (i.e., unfriendly; unagreeable), how likely are they to be incompetent (i.e., incapable; not smart)?" and "If this alien is known to be incompetent (i.e., incapable; not smart), how likely are they to be not warm (i.e., unfriendly; unagreeable)?" Responses will be collected on a scale from 1 to 9, where 1 represents "not at all likely" and 9 represents "very likely." The statistical models used will be identical to those in the main analysis.

table.title: The causal role of social status in positive trait coherence
table.research_questions:
We ask whether a novel social group’s status (advantaged vs. disadvantaged) selectively shapes positive trait coherence. Participants will be told about two fictitious social groups, the Bwisi (advantaged/higher status) and the Mwangai (disadvantaged/lower status), via a reading passage that describes the groups only in terms of socioeconomic status and does not describe or imply any personality traits for either group. Participants will then rate face identities that are independently and randomly labeled as Bwisi or Mwangai for each participant. Facial appearance will be parametrically manipulated along the validated facial information dimensions of trait judgments (Walker et al., 2018): the Agency dimension, which is closely related to competence, or the Communion dimension, which is closely related to warmth. 

We hypothesize a group difference in positive trait coherence. Specifically, we hypothesize cross dimension coherence between warmth and competence judgments will be stronger for faces labeled as the advantaged group than for faces labeled as the disadvantaged group. We further hypothesize that this group difference will be moderated by participants’ stereotype endorsement. Specifically, we hypothesize participants with stronger stereotype endorsement will show a larger gap between the dimension coherence for advantaged vs. disadvantaged group. 

As the pilot data showed that ratings were higher for the original, unmorphed faces than for the two manipulated levels (i.e., reduced and enhanced), we will measure trait coherence using two complementary approaches (see Dependent Variable below). First, the identity-based approach captures coherence in judgments attributable to face identity, independent of the shared effect of stimulus level. Second, the manipulation-based approach captures how strongly manipulated appearance on one trait dimension carries over to judgments of the other trait, following the approach of Hong and Freeman (2024). Rather than treating the three stimulus levels equivalently, these approaches either remove the shared effect of stimulus level or focus on the two manipulated extreme levels.
table.study_design_overview:
The study uses a fully within-subjects, repeated-measures design. There are no between-subjects experimental conditions. 

- Group (2 levels, within-subjects): Each of the 16 face identities is independently and randomly labeled as belonging to either the advantaged or disadvantaged group for each participant, with 8 identities assigned to each group. 
- Stimulus level (3 levels, within-subjects): Each identity is presented at three levels of trait relevant facial appearance: reduced, original, and enhanced, coded as Levels 1, 2, and 3, respectively. 
- Trait block (2 levels, within-subjects): Participants complete a Warmth block consisting of 16 identities × 3 Agency manipulated levels (48 trials) and a Competence block consisting of 16 identities × 3 Communion manipulated levels (48 trials). 

Block order, group assignment, and face/trial order are randomized across participants.
table.sample_size:
We will recruit 400 White participants via Prolific to minimize the potential influence of preexisting racial stereotypes toward the White face stimuli. This target is based on the sample size used in a similar study design by Hong and Freeman (2024). With an anticipated exclusion rate of approximately 20% based on the criteria described above, we expect a final viable sample of approximately 320 participants. 

With N = 320, the primary moderation test has 90% power to detect a correlation of r = .16, the effect observed for the identity-based index in our pilot data, and 80% power to detect r ≥ .14. Because the pilot estimate was based on a relatively small sample (N ≈ 70), the true effect may be smaller than the observed estimate. The two manipulation-based indices showed smaller pilot correlations (r = .02–.03), and are therefore expected to provide substantially less power. Accordingly, null findings, particularly for the manipulation-based indices, should be interpreted cautiously and should not be taken as evidence that the moderation effect is absent.
table.statistical_tests:
We will conduct two analyses of trait coherence. 

1. Group difference in coherence: For each coherence/transfer index, we will compare the index calculated for advantaged labeled identities with the corresponding index calculated for disadvantaged labeled identities using a paired t test. We predict greater coherence for the advantaged than the disadvantaged group and will use a one-tailed test. We will fully report descriptive statistics for all three indices. 

2. Moderation by stereotype endorsement: For each coherence/transfer index, we will calculate an advantaged minus disadvantaged coherence gap (i.e., index({Advantaged}) − index({Disadvantaged})) and regress this gap on participants’ stereotype endorsement. We will test two measures of stereotype endorsement, each using a one-tailed test in the predicted positive direction. The primary moderator is the difference between participants’ explicit competence stereotype ratings of the advantaged and disadvantaged groups. The secondary moderator combines this competence stereotype gap with warmth stereotype gap to provide a broader measure of stereotype endorsement across the two trait dimensions.
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.design_dependent_variables:
We will compute three coherence/transfer indices per participant, separately for the eight face identities labeled as the advantaged group and the eight labeled as the disadvantaged group. These indices fall into two complementary approaches: an identity-based approach resulting in one index and a manipulation-based approach resulting in two indices. 

Identity-based approach: Our primary confirmatory measure captures coherence attributable to face identity, independent of the shared effect of stimulus level. For each of the three stimulus levels, we mean-center the eight identities’ warmth ratings around the mean warmth rating at that level, and separately mean center the competence ratings around the mean competence rating at that level. We then pool the centered ratings across the three levels, and calculate the Pearson correlation between centered warmth and competence ratings. The resulting correlation is Fisher z transformed for inferential testing. The averaging procedure reduces measurement error and uses the full range of manipulated appearance, not discarding any level (unlike the manipulation-based indices, which drop Level 2). 

Manipulation-based approach: Two secondary confirmatory measures capture transfer from one trait dimension to the other. Both use only the two manipulated extreme levels (Level 1, reduced; Level 3, enhanced), excluding the original, unmorphed faces at Level 2. The warmth to competence transfer slope is calculated as [mean competence rating at Level 3 − mean competence rating at Level 1] / 2 for the Communion manipulated stimuli. This indexes the extent to which warmth relevant facial appearance carries over to competence judgments. The competence to warmth transfer slope is calculated analogously using warmth ratings for the Agency manipulated stimuli. This indexes the extent to which competence relevant facial appearance carries over to warmth judgments. 

All three indices are computed separately for the advantaged and disadvantaged labeled faces within each participant.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants will be excluded from all analyses if they meet either of the following criteria: 

1. Fail the status manipulation check: Participants will be excluded if they rate the disadvantaged group as higher in status than the advantaged group. 
2. Show no response variability: Participants will be excluded if they give the same rating on every trial within a trait block, indicating insufficient engagement with the rating task.

Methodology:
Greeble Stimuli.
Multi-dimensional object stimuli, such as Greebles (Gauthier & Tarr, 1997), will serve as the images of fictious social being, e.g., “aliens”. To make it easier for participants to distinguish between the two groups, we will assign one skin color to one gender and another skin color to the other (e.g., blue and green). The color palette will have an equal spacing between colors corresponds to equal perceptual differences, controlling the perceived variance in the two groups' colors. Stimuli will be randomly assigned to either, say, the green or blue group.

Learning Phase.
Participants will be informed that they are going to be introduced to two groups of aliens to report on these new species. The task begins with a learning phase in which participants will view images of 36 Greebles paired with unique behaviors. Each pair will be presented once, resulting in a total of 36 trials. Half of the Greebles will be paired with low-capability behaviors (e.g., has difficulty keeping track of their finances), and the other half will be paired with medium-capability behaviors (e.g., eats an apple every day). The assignment of blue and green Greebles to the disadvantaged or advantaged group will be randomized. Participants will view the Greeble behaviors in random order at their own pace and will be asked to visualize the alien engaging in the described behavior on each trial.

Attention check (understanding of group categorization):
To ensure that participants correctly associate specific behaviors with designated groups as intended by the manipulation, we will include four questions in the manipulation check. Participants will be asked to identify which Greeble is most likely to exhibit a specific behavior by choosing from Greeble group options. For example, they might answer the question, \"based on what you‘ve learned, which alien group is the individual most likely to belong to for this behavior: Gets confused by the rules of chess?\" Participants will receive feedback on their choices, which will reinforce the stereotypical associations with certain \"alien\" groups.

Conceptual halo effect.
Next, participants will engage in a conceptual trait association task. In this task, they will assess pairwise conceptual associations for both the advantaged and disadvantaged groups. They will answer four questions in total, with two alien groups and two conceptual directions. They will answer questions such as \"If this alien is known to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable), how likely are they to be competent (i.e., capable; smart)?\" and \"If this alien is known to be competent (i.e., capable; smart), how likely are they to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable)?\". The question will be presented along with a picture of an alien from the green/blue group. The picture will be randomly selected from a set of images per group. This approach ensures that participants think at the individual level (rather than the group level), and helps to reduce any bias introduced by a specific alien image. Ratings will be given on a scale from 1 (not at all likely) to 9 (very likely), at the participants' own pace, with stimuli presented in random order.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 559 columns across 74 data files.
#### Issues Identified

28 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 74 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 12 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  10 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  2 of 12 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  4 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable (not counted against the traffic light).
-  14 installable dependencies detected.
- 113 statistics stored from the extracted output; 7 of 34 reported tests matched (20.6%).

ethics_statements: Each dataset was originally collected under a separate ethics approval: #4952 (Dataset 1) from Princeton University, and DERC-2023-October-06 (Dataset 2), DERC-2023-November-08 (Dataset 3), and DERC-2023-October-14 (Dataset 4) from the National University of Singapore.

The study was preregistered prior to data collection (March 12, 2025; https://osf.io/c5buj/overview?view_only=8490adec4cb54f6d958bfaed299a2b26) and received IRB approval from the National University of Singapore (protocol code: DERC-2024-September-22).

The study was preregistered prior to data collection (September 8, 2026; https://osf.io/f5hr2/overview?view_only=a7873b65c68b479eb67ee1a1dbba2030) and received IRB approval from the National University of Singapore (protocol code: DERC-2024-September-22).
live_data_statements: All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the study.
Participants were compensated for their participation either with course credit or monetary compensation, depending on the recruitment source.
Across all datasets, participants completed face-rating tasks followed by stereotype measures.
Following the rating task, participants completed a domain-specific measure of stereotype endorsement.
The study was conducted online via Amazon Mechanical Turk.
As shown in Figure 1, participants were first sorted by stereotype endorsement.
Within each iteration, overlapping windows of 20 participants were extracted to calculate warmth-competence correlations (step size = 1).
Sixty U.S. residents were recruited via Prolific.
We recruited 400 white U.S. residents via Prolific.

Participants were excluded if they failed the basic knowledge check (i.e., rating the disadvantaged group as higher in status than the advantaged group) or showed no variability in their face ratings (i.e., responding with the same rating across all trials).

After completing both rating blocks, participants completed the stereotype endorsement measure by rating each group separately on warmth and competence ("How warm/competent do you think the Bwisi/Mwangai are on average?") on 1-9 scales, with group order and trait order randomized.

Sixteen participants were excluded from the identity-based coherence test because they gave invariant ratings (the same rating to all 24 faces on either warmth or competence), making the correlation undefined.

When told an alien was warm, participants were less likely to infer competence if it belonged to the low-capability stereotype group (Mmedium = 6.78, SD = 1.30; Mlow = 4.35, SD = 1.59; F(1,48) = 57.32, p < .001, ηp² = 0.54, 95% CI [0.38, 0.66]).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 12 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 4 files (mental_health_02_interaction.Rmd, age_02_interaction.Rmd, gender_02_interaction.Rmd, econ_status_02_interaction.Rmd): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:8, File = c("age_01_iteration.Rmd", 
"econ_status_01_interation.Rmd", "gender_01_iteration.Rmd", "mental_health_01_iteration.Rmd", 
"study_5_analysis.Rmd", "analysis_all.Rmd", "data_analysis.R", 
"data_analysis.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 12 scripts: 2 ran without error, 4 errored, 2 timed out, 4 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("age_01_iteration.Rmd", "econ_status_01_interation.Rmd", 
"gender_01_iteration.Rmd", "mental_health_01_iteration.Rmd", 
"study_5_analysis.Rmd", "analysis_all.Rmd", "data_analysis.R", 
"data_analysis.Rmd", "mental_health_02_interaction.Rmd", "age_02_interaction.Rmd", 
"gender_02_interaction.Rmd", "econ_status_02_interaction.Rmd"
), Outcome = c("dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable", 
"timed_out", "timed_out", "dependency_unavailable", "ran_ok", 
"dependency_unavailable", "ran_ok", "errored", "errored", "errored", 
"errored"), Detail = c("dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable", 
"timeout", "timeout", "dependency_unavailable", "", "dependency_unavailable", 
"", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(3.9, 
3.8, 300.4, 300.4, 3.8, 5.1, 4.3, 8.7, 4.2, 3.9, 3.8, 3.9)), row.names = c(NA, 
-12L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**4 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("age_01_iteration.Rmd", "econ_status_01_interation.Rmd", 
"study_5_analysis.Rmd", "data_analysis.R")), row.names = c(NA, 
-4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**2 scripts use functions from packages they do not load themselves.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. text.text: The halo effect reflects a fundamental bias in person perception: humans infer multiple positive qualities from a single trait, assuming traits cohere.
Here we show that this coherence depends on targets' social status and perceivers' stereotype endorsement.

Across four correlational datasets and two experiments examining gender, age, economic status, mental health, and novel groups (total N = 623), perceivers high in stereotype endorsement showed weaker coherence between warmth and competence inferences for disadvantaged than for advantaged targets.

In preregistered experiments with novel groups, learning a low-competence stereotype weakened conceptual trait coherence, and after learning only about group status, the coherence gap scaled with the competence stereotypes participants formed.
These findings reveal a subtle form of bias: stereotypes fragment the cognitive scaffolding of impression formation, imposing unequal burdens on members of marginalized groups.
While navigating the social world, people spontaneously attribute various traits to others upon viewing their faces.

Although effortless, these face-based judgments can shape high-stakes real-world outcomes, such as leader selection (Antonakis & Eubanks, 2017), criminal sentencing (Wilson & Rule, 2015), and election results (Todorov et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Although effortless, these face-based judgments can shape high-stakes real-world outcomes, such as leader selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Antonakis & Eubanks, 2017)</ref>, criminal sentencing <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Wilson & Rule, 2015)</ref>, and election results <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Todorov et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A body of research suggests that such judgments are organized around a small number of fundamental dimensions of social evaluation: others' intentions (e.g., warmth, trustworthiness, communion) and their capacity to enact those intentions (e.g., competence, dominance, agency), a structure found across impression domains (Fiske et al., 2002 (Fiske et al., , 2007;; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008; Rosenberg et al., 1968; Todorov et al., 2008).
text.formatted: A body of research suggests that such judgments are organized around a small number of fundamental dimensions of social evaluation: others' intentions (e.g., warmth, trustworthiness, communion) and their capacity to enact those intentions (e.g., competence, dominance, agency), a structure found across impression domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiske et al., 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fiske et al., , 2007;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Rosenberg et al., 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Todorov et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The constructs grouped under each dimension are related but not interchangeable (Abele et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The constructs grouped under each dimension are related but not interchangeable <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abele et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Here we focus on warmth and competence, the dimensions most closely tied to group stereotypes (Fiske et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Here we focus on warmth and competence, the dimensions most closely tied to group stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiske et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, these fundamental dimensions are not evaluated independently.
Impressions of one trait can influence judgments of others, giving rise to interconnected patterns of trait inference (Freeman & Lin, 2025).
text.formatted: Impressions of one trait can influence judgments of others, giving rise to interconnected patterns of trait inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Freeman & Lin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The halo effect represents a prominent form of this interconnectedness, whereby positive impressions on one trait generalize to other traits (Rosenberg et al., 1968; Thorndike, 1920).
text.formatted: The halo effect represents a prominent form of this interconnectedness, whereby positive impressions on one trait generalize to other traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rosenberg et al., 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Thorndike, 1920)</ref>.

text.text: For example, moral violation lowers perceived competence (Stellar & Willer, 2018).
text.formatted: For example, moral violation lowers perceived competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Stellar & Willer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In the opposite direction, competence information leads to perceived warmth (Chen & Guo, 2021).
text.formatted: In the opposite direction, competence information leads to perceived warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chen & Guo, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This cross-trait alignment may serve as a cognitive shortcut, allowing people to construct rich social impressions from limited information.

Emerging evidence suggests that positive trait coherence in person perception can shift with characteristics of the perceiver and the social context, including the personality of people in the perceiver's region (Oh et al., 2022), idiosyncratic beliefs about trait associations (Stolier et al., 2018 (Stolier et al., , 2020)), racial and gender stereotypes (Xie et al., 2021), and targets' social group memberships (Collova et al., 2019; Hong & Freeman, 2024; Oh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Emerging evidence suggests that positive trait coherence in person perception can shift with characteristics of the perceiver and the social context, including the personality of people in the perceiver's region <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Oh et al., 2022)</ref>, idiosyncratic beliefs about trait associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Stolier et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Stolier et al., , 2020))</ref>, racial and gender stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2021)</ref>, and targets' social group memberships <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Collova et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hong & Freeman, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Oh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These findings raise the possibility that positive trait coherence is a malleable structure shaped by both perceiver-and target-related factors, rather than a stable feature of social perception.
Among these influences, social group membership may be particularly consequential because it changes the meaning of trait information itself.
For example, the association between trustworthiness and dominance becomes more negative for outgroup faces but more positive for ingroup faces (Hong & Freeman, 2024).
text.formatted: For example, the association between trustworthiness and dominance becomes more negative for outgroup faces but more positive for ingroup faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hong & Freeman, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, group stereotypes can shape how people infer one trait from another.

When a diagnostically relevant trait is omitted and only a positive evaluation on another dimension is provided, perceivers tend to infer a negative value on the unmentioned dimension; importantly, this tendency is stronger for female than male targets (Kervyn et al., 2012).
text.formatted: When a diagnostically relevant trait is omitted and only a positive evaluation on another dimension is provided, perceivers tend to infer a negative value on the unmentioned dimension; importantly, this tendency is stronger for female than male targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kervyn et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that stereotype-based processes may disrupt positive trait coherence selectively across social groups, particularly when targets belong to socially disadvantaged categories.
More broadly, decades of stereotype research suggest that group stereotypes often depart from the positive coherence observed in individual-level inferences.

Whereas warmth and competence perceptions tend to covary positively, group and cultural stereotypes frequently encode systematic warmth-competence inversions that violate the halo-effect principle (Judd et al., 2005; Kervyn et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Whereas warmth and competence perceptions tend to covary positively, group and cultural stereotypes frequently encode systematic warmth-competence inversions that violate the halo-effect principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Judd et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kervyn et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For example, older adults are seen as warm but incompetent (Cuddy et al., 2007; Fiske et al., 2002).
text.formatted: For example, older adults are seen as warm but incompetent <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cuddy et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fiske et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Across 23 social groups in the U.S., 20 were consistently perceived as either more competent than warm or warmer than competent (Fiske et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Across 23 social groups in the U.S., 20 were consistently perceived as either more competent than warm or warmer than competent <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiske et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: This raises an apparent paradox: stereotypes generally exhibit a compensatory structure, with warmth and competence negatively related, whereas extensive evidence supports a halo effect in person perception.

Importantly, stereotype judgments can also vary across perceivers (Koch et al., 2020), highlighting the importance of considering individual differences in how stereotyperelated information is integrated into social impressions.
text.formatted: Importantly, stereotype judgments can also vary across perceivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Koch et al., 2020)</ref>, highlighting the importance of considering individual differences in how stereotyperelated information is integrated into social impressions.

text.text: Existing group-level theories have mapped where groups fall within the warmth-competence space, but have paid less attention to how the relationship between these dimensions itself may become a source of bias.
In the current research, we propose that stereotype endorsement shapes how trait information is integrated across social groups.
Specifically, the difference in positive trait coherence between advantaged and disadvantaged targets should depend on how strongly perceivers endorse the relevant group stereotypes.
Perceivers who strongly endorse these stereotypes may apply group-specific expectations to disadvantaged targets, weakening positive trait coherence for these targets relative to advantaged targets.
This framework yields three predictions.
First, unlike group-level theories that assume consensual stereotypes, we predict that the trait coherence gap will vary continuously with individual stereotype endorsement.
Perceivers with stronger stereotype endorsement should show a larger coherence gap between advantaged and disadvantaged groups.

Second, if stereotype-based processes shape the integration of trait information, similar patterns of fragmentation should emerge across diverse social categories despite variation in specific stereotype content.
Third, trait coherence should be disrupted merely by learning that targets belong to disadvantaged groups, even for novel groups, to the extent that perceivers form stereotypes about them.

We test this framework across two studies (four datasets and two experiments) examining trait coherence patterns in gender, age, economic status, mental health, and experimentally created novel groups.
We pooled data from Study 1, Datasets 2-4 for an integrative analysis of individual-level coherence shifts.
Complementing this, we examine continuous structural changes within each specific domain (Study 1, Datasets 1-4).

Study 2 extends to novel groups without preexisting cultural stereotypes by manipulating stereotype "knowledge" (learned group-trait associations; Study 2a) and social status (Study 2b) in fictitious social groups.

Together, these studies test whether stereotype endorsement systematically predicts weaker warmth-competence coherence for disadvantaged than advantaged groups, and whether this asymmetry can emerge even for novel groups following minimal information about group disadvantage.
We analyzed four independent datasets spanning diverse social domains (see Table 1).
text.formatted: We analyzed four independent datasets spanning diverse social domains (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Each dataset was originally collected under a separate ethics approval: #4952 (Dataset 1) from Princeton University, and DERC-2023-October-06 (Dataset 2) , DERC-2023-November-08 (Dataset 3), and DERC-2023-October-14 (Dataset 4) from the National University of Singapore.
Secondary use of these data for the present analyses fell within the scope of the original approved protocol.
Datasets 2-4 were originally collected as part of undergraduate research projects that have not been published.
They were subsequently reused for the present analyses, which address different research questions using different analytical approaches.
These analyses were not preregistered.
Participants.
Dataset 1 analyzed publicly available data from 71 U.S.-based participants (35 females, 36 males) drawn from a larger study involving face-based trait ratings (Oh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Dataset 1 analyzed publicly available data from 71 U.S.-based participants (35 females, 36 males) drawn from a larger study involving face-based trait ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Oh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Datasets 2-4 were conducted in Singapore with predominantly ethnic-Chinese samples: Dataset 2 (N = 61, Mage = 23.00, SDage = 2.76; 47 females, 14 males; 61 ethnic Chinese); Dataset 3 (N = 64, Mage = 23.81, SDage = 8.05; 38 females, 25 males, 1 nonbinary; 55 ethnic Chinese, 6 Indian, 1 Sinhalese, 1 Eurasian, 1 Vietnamese); Dataset 4 (N = 76, Mage = 22.04, SDage = 1.97; 47 females, 29 males; 76 ethnic Chinese).
Gender was self-reported by participants.
Data on participants' socioeconomic status were not collected.
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the study.
Participants were compensated for their participation either with course credit or monetary compensation, depending on the recruitment source.
Across all datasets, participants completed face-rating tasks followed by stereotype measures.
Consistent with the theoretical framework of the Stereotype Content Model (Fiske et al., 2002), we analyzed ratings of warmth and competence.
text.formatted: Consistent with the theoretical framework of the Stereotype Content Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fiske et al., 2002)</ref>, we analyzed ratings of warmth and competence.

text.text: In datasets where these exact labels were unavailable, we operationalized these dimensions using the most theoretically aligned proxies (e.g., trustworthiness for warmth, intelligence for competence).
Group membership was conveyed through facial cues (Datasets 1-2), explicit labels (Dataset 3), or clothing cues (Dataset 4).
Following the rating task, participants completed a domain-specific measure of stereotype endorsement.
Table 1 presents an overview of the datasets.

Forty Chinese faces were presented: 20 older adults (60-70 years, Mage = 65, SDage = 2.58) and 20 younger adults (19-30 years, Mage = 23, SDage = 3.39) from the Tsinghua Facial Expression Database (Yang et al., 2020) and East Asian Facial Expression Database (Tu et al., 2018).

text.text: Participants rated all faces in two blocks (warmth, then competence) on 1-9 scales while relying on first impressions.

Stereotype endorsement was measured using the Aging Semantic Differential (ASD; Rosencranz & McNevin, 1969), a widely used instrument for assessing younger adults' explicit attitudes toward aging (Ayalon et al., 2019). groomed" for Major Depressive Disorder).

text.text: The symptom-absent labels described mildly negative situation-induced changes in mood or behavior (e.g., "This person usually sleeps well but has recently mentioned experiencing some sleeplessness due to stress"; "This person was upset with someone for breaking a promise"), and were matched in length and content specificity to symptom labels.
Participants rated all faces on trustworthiness and competence (order counterbalanced) on 1-9 scales and saw each face with both label types.
Stereotype endorsement was measured using the 9-item Internalized Stigma of Mental Illness Inventory (Hammer & Toland, 2017).
text.formatted: Stereotype endorsement was measured using the 9-item Internalized Stigma of Mental Illness Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hammer & Toland, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The study was conducted online.

Forty faces from standardized databases, the Chicago Face Database India Extension and Tsinghua Facial Expression Database (Lakshmi et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020), were presented paired with clothing indicating rich or poor status.
text.formatted: Forty faces from standardized databases, the Chicago Face Database India Extension and Tsinghua Facial Expression Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lakshmi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Yang et al., 2020)</ref>, were presented paired with clothing indicating rich or poor status.

text.text: Participants rated all faces on warmth and competence (order counterbalanced) on 1-9 scales.

Stereotype endorsement was measured using eight questions about societal perceptions of rich and poor individuals (e.g., "As viewed by most people in Singapore, how competent are the rich people?") on 1-5 scales (Cuddy et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Stereotype endorsement was measured using eight questions about societal perceptions of rich and poor individuals (e.g., "As viewed by most people in Singapore, how competent are the rich people?") on 1-5 scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cuddy et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Because these items ask participants to report perceived societal consensus about rich and poor people as social categories, they are conceptually distinct from the face-rating task, in which participants rated the warmth and competence of specific individuals.

Thus, the stereotype items capture group-level stereotype content, whereas the coherence outcome reflects the withinparticipant correlation between warmth and competence ratings across individual identities.

To capture the ambivalent nature of economic-status stereotypes (i.e., that individuals with low economic status are perceived as warm but incompetent, whereas those with high economic status are perceived as competent but cold), we calculated two separate difference indices: a Warmth Stereotype Index, computed as the warmth rating of low-economic-status targets minus high-economic-status targets, and a Competence Stereotype Index, computed as the competence rating of high-economic-status targets minus low-economic-status targets.
Integrative data analysis.
To maximize statistical power and test domain-generality, we conducted an individual-level integrative data analysis across Datasets 2-4.
Dataset 1 was excluded from this aggregation because its between-subjects design (where participants rated only a single trait) precluded the calculation of within-participant trait correlations.
To ensure comparability, all stereotype endorsement scores and trait ratings were z-standardized within each dataset.

For the Economic Status dataset, we summed the warmth and competence difference indices; to align this bipolar metric with the unipolar scales of other datasets, we included only positive values indicating alignment with cultural stereotypes favoring the higheconomic-status group.
We fitted a linear mixed-effects model to predict the coherence gap (Advantaged minus Disadvantaged Fisher's z-transformed warmth-competence correlation) from stereotype endorsement.
This model included random intercepts for datasets.
Although we initially specified random slopes for stereotype endorsement, this resulted in a singular fit.

Given that random slopes did not significantly improve model fit compared with a random-intercept-only model (χ² = 0.20, p = .906), we removed them to resolve the singularity and report results from the final model with random intercepts for datasets.
Because the slopes were constrained to be equal across datasets, the model tests whether a common slope fits the pooled data, rather than whether the association is equivalent across domains.
This association remained essentially identical after controlling for group differences in rating variability (Supplementary Information Section 1.1).
Complementing the integrative analysis, we employed a sliding window approach to visualize continuous structural changes and detect domain-specific nuances (including Dataset 1).
This approach generates robust estimates through iterative resampling.

By aggregating participants with similar levels of endorsement, this strategy facilitates the detection of graded trends across participant groups and yields a continuous characterization of how coherence varies along the endorsement spectrum, avoiding the loss of information inherent in discretizing participants into arbitrary groups (Xia et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By aggregating participants with similar levels of endorsement, this strategy facilitates the detection of graded trends across participant groups and yields a continuous characterization of how coherence varies along the endorsement spectrum, avoiding the loss of information inherent in discretizing participants into arbitrary groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Xia et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Zhao et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As shown in Figure 1, participants were first sorted by stereotype endorsement.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>, participants were first sorted by stereotype endorsement.

text.text: To ensure that results were not driven by any single local ordering of participants along this continuum, we conducted 1,000 iterations, each involving a random reshuffling of participant order within identical stereotype levels.
Within each iteration, overlapping windows of 20 participants were extracted to calculate warmth-competence correlations (step size = 1).

For Datasets 2-4, we computed correlations using residuals derived from intercept-only mixed-effects models with crossed random intercepts for participants and faces, thereby partitioning out individual response biases and target consensus effects.
For Dataset 1 (between-subjects), correlations were calculated based on the vector of face means within each window.
Each window generated two trait correlations (one per target group), paired with the mean stereotype endorsement of that window.
Within each iteration, moderation analyses tested the interaction between stereotype endorsement and target group using the sliding window subgroups.
Johnson-Neyman analyses were applied within each iteration to identify regions along the stereotype continuum where group differences in trait coherence were statistically significant.
Finally, estimates were aggregated across the 1,000 iterations to characterize the stability of moderation effects and the robustness of the identified Johnson-Neyman regions.
For each iteration, we also computed ηp² for the interaction using the fixed degrees of freedom for each domain.

We report the mean ηp² and 95% CI across the 1,000 iterations. specific variability. e, Example showing how the warmth-competence correlation varies across stereotype levels for advantaged and disadvantaged groups. f, Johnson-Neyman analysis of regression coefficients.
We next experimentally tested whether learning stereotype-relevant information is sufficient to alter trait coherence in novel groups without preexisting cultural stereotypes.
In Study 2a, we focused on conceptual trait coherence where target groups were represented by non-human stimuli, precluding the direct assessment of trait impressions from individuals (i.e., faces).

Conceptual trait associations have been shown to shape impression coherence (Stolier et al., 2018 (Stolier et al., , 2020)), providing a way to test whether learned group-trait associations can alter the coherence between positive traits.
text.formatted: Conceptual trait associations have been shown to shape impression coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Stolier et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Stolier et al., , 2020))</ref>, providing a way to test whether learned group-trait associations can alter the coherence between positive traits.

text.text: The study was preregistered prior to data collection (March 12, 2025; https://osf.io/c5buj/overview?view_only=8490adec4cb54f6d958bfaed299a2b26) and received IRB approval from the National University of Singapore (protocol code: DERC-2024-September-22).
text.formatted: The study was preregistered prior to data collection (March 12, 2025; <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/c5buj/overview?view_only=8490adec4cb54f6d958bfaed299a2b26">https://osf.io/c5buj/overview?view_only=8490adec4cb54f6d958bfaed299a2b26</ref>) and received IRB approval from the National University of Singapore (protocol code: DERC-2024-September-22).

text.text: Participants.
Sixty U.S. residents were recruited via Prolific.
Sample size was determined a priori using G*Power for a repeated-measures ANOVA with within-subject factors.

Because prior data were unavailable to estimate the correlation among repeated measures, we assumed a correlation of .50, corresponding to the midpoint of the typical range reported for repeated-measures designs (.30-.70).
Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25), α = .05, and 95% power, the analysis indicated a required sample of 54 participants.
We therefore recruited 60 participants to allow for approximately 10% exclusions.

Deviating from the preregistration, only group competence ratings were used as a check of stereotype learning, because the learning materials manipulated only competence-related behaviors while warmth-related information was matched across groups.
After exclusions for manipulation check failures, 49 participants remained (Mage = 38.18, SDage = 12.69; 29 females, 20 males; 35 white, 5 Black or African American, 5 Asian, 4 Other).
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the study.
Participants received monetary compensation for their participation.
Stimuli.
Multi-dimensional "Greeble" stimuli (Gauthier & Tarr, 1997) represented fictitious aliens, with color (blue/green) indicating group membership.
text.formatted: Multi-dimensional "Greeble" stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gauthier & Tarr, 1997)</ref> represented fictitious aliens, with color (blue/green) indicating group membership.

text.text: Using Greebles eliminates preexisting stereotypes that might confound results with real social groups.
This allowed us to isolate the causal effect of learned group information on trait coherence.

Group stereotypes were taught with behavioral descriptions from the Delaware Behavior Database (Mende-Siedlecki & Havlicek, 2025), which provides normative competence and warmth ratings for each behavior.
text.formatted: Group stereotypes were taught with behavioral descriptions from the Delaware Behavior Database (Mende-Siedlecki & Havlicek, 2025), which provides normative competence and warmth ratings for each behavior.

text.text: Based on these ratings, we calculated the corresponding validation statistics, which showed that the selected behaviors differed on competence (capability: F = 281.20, p < .001; intelligence: F = 112.56, p < .001) while being matched on warmth (sociability: F = 0.03, p = .876; trustworthiness: F = 0.13, p = .716), providing precise experimental control over the specific dimensions being manipulated.
text.formatted: Based on these ratings, we calculated the corresponding validation statistics, which showed that the selected behaviors differed on competence (capability: F = 281.20, p < .001; intelligence: F = 112.56, p < .001) while being matched on warmth (sociability: F = 0.03, p = .876; trustworthiness: F = 0.13, p = .716), providing precise experimental control over the specific dimensions being manipulated.

text.text: See Supplementary Table 2 for all behaviors presented.
text.formatted: See Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref> for all behaviors presented.

text.text: Procedure.
In the learning phase, participants viewed 36 Greebles-behavior pairs.

To approximate the probabilistic nature of real-world stereotype learning, in which group members do not uniformly conform to a group stereotype, 16 of 18 members of the low-capability stereotype group were paired with low-capability behaviors, while 16 of 18 members of the medium-capability stereotype group were paired with medium-capability behaviors.
The remaining two members in each group were paired with behaviors from the other capability level.
This procedure is consistent with research showing that people can learn and apply social stereotypes from imperfect group-behavior associations (Lick et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This procedure is consistent with research showing that people can learn and apply social stereotypes from imperfect group-behavior associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lick et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We focused on capability because competence is closely associated with social status in established models of intergroup relations (Cuddy et al., 2009; Fiske, 1993).
text.formatted: We focused on capability because competence is closely associated with social status in established models of intergroup relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cuddy et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fiske, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: This allowed us to create systematic differences in competence-related behavioral information while holding warmth-related information constant.

We used low-versus medium-capability behaviors, rather than low-versus high-capability behaviors, to model a more moderate group difference in which one group is characterized by relatively lower capability and the other by more ordinary levels of capability, rather than contrasting a disadvantaged group with an exceptionally high-performing group.
Learning was reinforced via feedback on four association questions.

On each question, participants viewed a behavior (e.g., "still gets lost in town after being there two years") and indicated which group an individual displaying that behavior was most likely to belong to.
Participants then received feedback indicating the correct group-behavior association.

Finally, participants rated (1) the likelihood of inferring one positive trait from another for a single Greeble randomly selected from the stimulus set (e.g., "This alien is known to be competent (i.e., capable; smart), how likely are they to be warm (i.e., friendly; agreeable)?").
Ratings were made on 9-point scales for both groups in both inference directions, indexing trait coherence as the extent to which one positive trait implies another.
Participants also rated (2) overall group warmth and competence to measure stereotype formation.

We conducted within-subjects ANOVAs to compare the low-and medium-capability stereotype groups on stereotype ratings and positive trait generalizations (coherence), examining both inference directions (warm-to-competent and competent-to-warm).
text.formatted: We conducted within-subjects ANOVAs to compare the low-and medium-capability stereotype groups on stereotype ratings and positive trait generalizations (coherence), examining both inference directions <ref type="bibr">(warm-to-competent and competent-to-warm)</ref>.

text.text: Bonferroni correction was applied for multiple comparisons.
As a robustness check, we included all participants regardless of the manipulation check, and the results remained unchanged; these analyses are reported in the Supplementary Information Section 2.
In Study 2b, we further isolated the effect of social status by having participants learn about group status without providing any stereotype-relevant trait information.
We then assessed participants' impressions of individual group members using a face-rating task.

The study was preregistered prior to data collection (September 8, 2026; https://osf.io/f5hr2/overview?view_only=a7873b65c68b479eb67ee1a1dbba2030) and received IRB approval from the National University of Singapore (protocol code: DERC-2024-September-22).

text.text: Participants.
We recruited 400 white U.S. residents via Prolific.
We restricted recruitment to white participants to limit the potential influence of preexisting racial stereotypes on judgments.

The target sample size was predetermined as approximately 300 participants, following the design of a similar study by Hong and Freeman (2024, Study 2), with an anticipated exclusion rate of approximately 20%.

Participants were excluded if they failed the basic knowledge check (i.e., rating the disadvantaged group as higher in status than the advantaged group) or showed no variability in their face ratings (i.e., responding with the same rating across all trials).
After exclusions, 302 participants remained (Mage = 43.32, SDage = 12.70; 159 females, 142 males, 1 prefer not to say).
All participants provided informed consent before taking part in the study.
Participants received monetary compensation for their participation.
Stimuli.
We used 16 white male face identities from the Basel Face Database (Walker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: We used 16 white male face identities from the Basel Face Database <ref type="bibr">(Walker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Faces were restricted to a single race and sex to prevent race-or gender-based stereotypes from confounding the effects of the experimentally assigned group labels.
Each identity was independently manipulated along the Communion and Agency dimensions, corresponding to the warmth and competence dimensions examined throughout this paper.
This resulted in three stimulus levels for each dimension: reduced, original, and enhanced (±3 SD from the original identity).
For each participant, eight identities were randomly assigned to the advantaged group and the remaining eight to the disadvantaged group.
Group assignments were independently re-randomized for each participant.
Procedure.
Participants first read a passage introducing a small fictitious country with two social groups, the Bwisi and the Mwangai.
The passage was loosely adapted from previous social status manipulations using unfamiliar groups (Caprariello et al., 2009; Conway et al., 1996; Nier et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The passage was loosely adapted from previous social status manipulations using unfamiliar groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caprariello et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Conway et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Nier et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: It described the Bwisi as the default group with higher social status and the Mwangai as a marked minority group with lower social status and fewer resources.
No personality traits or behavioral tendencies were attributed to either group.
Straightforward comprehension questions were embedded throughout the passage, and participants could not proceed until they answered them correctly.
The full passage and comprehension questions are provided in Supplementary Information Section 3.
Participants then completed two blocks of face rating trials, following the procedure used by Hong and Freeman (2024).
text.formatted: Participants then completed two blocks of face rating trials, following the procedure used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hong and Freeman (2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the competence-to-warmth transfer block, participants rated the warmth of all 16 identities, each shown at three levels of Agency-related, competence relevant appearance, resulting in 48 trials.

In the warmth-to-competence transfer block, participants rated the competence of the same 16 identities, each shown at three levels of Communion-related, warmth relevant appearance, resulting in another 48 trials.
Group membership labels were displayed alongside each face.
Block order was randomized, and trial order was randomized within each block.

After completing both rating blocks, participants completed the stereotype endorsement measure by rating each group separately on warmth and competence ("How warm/competent do you think the Bwisi/Mwangai are on average?") on 1-9 scales, with group order and trait order randomized.
Measuring stereotype endorsement after the face-rating blocks ensured that exposure to these items could not shape face judgments.
Finally, participants rated the overall social status of the two groups as a manipulation check and provided demographic information.

As preregistered, we computed three trait coherence/transfer indices per participant, separately for the eight face identities labeled as the advantaged group and the eight labeled as the disadvantaged group.

Because pilot data indicated that mean ratings were higher for the original, unmorphed faces than for either manipulated level (reduced or enhanced), rather than showing a simple linear increase across stimulus levels, we used two complementary approaches that treated the original and manipulated stimuli differently.
The identity-based approach provided the primary confirmatory measure and captured coherence attributable to face identity while accounting for the shared effect of stimulus level.

For each stimulus level, we mean-centered the eight identities' warmth ratings around the mean warmth rating at that level and separately mean-centered the competence ratings around the mean competence rating at that level.

Because warmth ratings were made for Agency-manipulated images and competence ratings for Communion-manipulated images, the paired warmth and competence ratings at the reduced and enhanced levels came from two different images of the same identity, whereas at the original level both ratings were of the same unmorphed image.
Ratings were thus paired by identity and stimulus level rather than by image.

We then pooled the centered ratings across the three stimulus levels and calculated the Pearson correlation between centered warmth and competence ratings, with correlations Fisher z-transformed for inferential testing.
This approach incorporated all three stimulus levels and therefore retained the full range of manipulated appearance.

The manipulation-based approach provided two secondary confirmatory measures of transfer between trait dimensions and used only the two manipulated extreme levels (reduced and enhanced), excluding the original, unmorphed faces.

The warmth-to-competence transfer slope was calculated as (mean competence rating at the enhanced level -mean competence rating at the reduced level) / 2 for the Communion-manipulated stimuli, indexing the extent to which warmth-relevant facial appearance transferred to competence judgments.

The competenceto-warmth transfer slope was calculated analogously using warmth ratings for the Agencymanipulated stimuli, indexing the extent to which competence-relevant facial appearance transferred to warmth judgments.
For each of the three indices, we conducted two preregistered tests.

First, we compared the index for advantaged-labeled identities with the corresponding index for disadvantagedlabeled identities using a paired t-test, with a one-tailed prediction of greater coherence for the advantaged group.

Second, we calculated each participant's advantaged-minus-disadvantaged coherence gap and regressed it on two preregistered moderators of stereotype endorsement, each tested one-tailed in the predicted positive direction.
The primary moderator was the difference between participants' explicit competence-stereotype ratings of the advantaged and disadvantaged groups.
The secondary moderator combined this competence stereotype gap with the warmth stereotype gap to provide a broader measure of stereotype endorsement across both trait dimensions.

Sixteen participants were excluded from the identity-based coherence test because they gave invariant ratings (the same rating to all 24 faces on either warmth or competence), making the correlation undefined.
Integrative analysis (Datasets 2-4).

We first tested our core hypothesis that higher stereotype endorsement predicts a wider gap in trait coherence between advantaged and disadvantaged groups using a combined dataset across Datasets 2-4.
Dataset 1 was excluded from this individual-level aggregation due to its between-subjects design.
While individual studies varied in statistical power, the pooled analysis revealed a small but reliable structural shift.

A linear mixed-effects model confirmed that stronger stereotype endorsement significantly predicted a larger difference in warmth-competence coherence between advantaged and disadvantaged groups, β = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 0.30], SE = 0.07, t = 2.09, p = .038 (Figure 2).

text.text: These findings suggest that the group difference in warmth-competence coherence was larger among perceivers with stronger stereotype endorsement. the predicted fixed effect from the linear mixed-effects model, illustrating the consistent overall trend.
Colored lines represent descriptive linear fits for each individual study domain to visualize consistency.
Dataset 1 is not included because its between-subjects design does not permit participant-level trait correlations.
To examine domain-specific patterns and include Dataset 1, we employed a sliding window analysis with 1,000 iterations.

This approach stabilizes estimates by averaging out variability due to local ordering and idiosyncratic rating patterns, preserving the continuous nature of the stereotype endorsement spectrum (Figure 1).

text.text: Across domains of social categorization, a consistent finding emerged: at high levels of stereotype endorsement, advantaged groups showed stronger warmth-competence coherence in face-based judgments than disadvantaged groups (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Across domains of social categorization, a consistent finding emerged: at high levels of stereotype endorsement, advantaged groups showed stronger warmth-competence coherence in face-based judgments than disadvantaged groups (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>).

text.text: This pattern held across three of the four datasets.

Formally, the interaction between group type and stereotype endorsement was statistically significant across all datasets employing within-subjects designs: Age, F(1, 40) = 56.11, p < .001, ηp² = 0.58, 95% CI [0.53, 0.63]; Mental Health, F(1, 86) = 8.86, p = .004, ηp² = 0.10, 95% CI [0.04, 0.18]; and Economic Status, whether indexed by warmth, F(1, 110) = 43.10, p < .001, ηp² = 0.38, 95% CI [0.12, 0.65], or competence, F(1, 110) = 53.41, p < .001, ηp² = 0.41, 95% CI [0.13, 0.67].

text.text: Dataset 1 (Gender), which employed a between-subjects design, showed a consistent directional trend but did not reach statistical significance, F(1, 285.67) = 2.66, p = .104, ηp² = 0.01, 95% CI [0.00, 0.03], likely reflecting reduced statistical power compared to the within-subjects designs.

Critically, this coherence measure captures the relationship between traits rather than their overall level, and therefore cannot be reduced to a general tendency to rate the disadvantaged group more negatively.

Having established that trait association fragments differently for advantaged versus disadvantaged group members among perceivers high in stereotype endorsement, we next examined whether learning a group stereotype is sufficient to weaken conceptual positive trait coherence, that is, the tendency to infer one positive trait from knowledge of another.

Conceptual associations can shape impression coherence (Stolier et al., 2018 (Stolier et al., , 2020)); these associations can mediate the effect of target group membership on correlations among trait impressions (Hong & Freeman, 2024).
text.formatted: Conceptual associations can shape impression coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Stolier et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Stolier et al., , 2020))</ref>; these associations can mediate the effect of target group membership on correlations among trait impressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hong & Freeman, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Study 2a experimentally manipulated stereotype knowledge about novel groups to test whether learning group stereotypes associated with social status (a proxy of competence level) disrupts this natural positive coherence.
Participants learned about two groups of novel aliens (Greebles; Figure 4a) by viewing 36 alien-behavior pairs.
text.formatted: Participants learned about two groups of novel aliens (Greebles; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4a</ref>) by viewing 36 alien-behavior pairs.

text.text: Most members of one group performed low-capability behaviors (e.g., "still gets lost in town after being there two years"), whereas most members of the other performed behaviors reflecting more ordinary levels of capability (e.g., "eats an apple every day").
The two sets of behaviors were matched on warmth.
Participants then judged how likely a group member known to possess one positive trait (e.g., competence) was to possess another (e.g., warmth) (Figure 4b).
text.formatted: Participants then judged how likely a group member known to possess one positive trait (e.g., competence) was to possess another (e.g., warmth) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4b</ref>).

text.text: Finally, they rated each group's overall warmth and competence.
Despite manipulating only competence while matching warmth in the learning materials, the low-capability stereotype group was perceived as both less competent (Mmedium = 7.29 vs.
Mlow = 3.39; F(1,48) = 207.18, p < .001, ηp² = 0.81, 95% CI [0.73, 0.86]) and less warm than the medium-capability stereotype group (Mmedium = 6.59 vs.

text.text: This spillover diverges from previous findings where dimensional compensation typically emerges when evaluating two groups comparatively (Judd et al., 2005).

text.text: Instead of a compensatory effect, our results suggest a generalization from competence to warmth, consistent with evidence that competence information can shape warmth judgments (Chen & Guo, 2021).

text.text: Alternatively, this spillover may be a methodological artifact driven by experimental order.

Because the stereotype ratings were collected after the positive trait generalization task, participants may have adjusted their warmth ratings to maintain evaluative consistency with their earlier responses.
Generalizations between warmth and competence were weaker for the low-capability stereotype group across both inference directions (Figure 4c).
text.formatted: Generalizations between warmth and competence were weaker for the low-capability stereotype group across both inference directions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4c</ref>).

text.text: When told an alien was warm, participants were less likely to infer competence if it belonged to the low-capability stereotype group (Mmedium = 6.78, SD = 1.30; Mlow = 4.35, SD = 1.59; F(1,48) = 57.32, p < .001, ηp² = 0.54, 95% CI [0.38, 0.66]).

text.text: Although the limited generalization from warmth to competence may reflect the emphasis on competence in the learning materials, the reverse pattern is more informative.

When participants learned that an alien from a low-capability stereotype group was highly competent, this positive trait was still less likely to generalize to warmth compared to the medium-capability stereotype group (Mmedium = 6.45, SD = 1.28; Mlow = 4.92, SD = 1.63; F(1,48) = 34.40, p < .001, ηp² = 0.42, 95% CI [0.24, 0.56]).
