text.text: This pattern suggests that learning a negative competence-related stereotype can weaken the natural generalization of positive traits, preventing favorable qualities from reinforcing one another.
While these findings are consistent with our central claim, a potential issue remains.

Because participants perceived the low-capability stereotype group as lower in warmth, despite matched materials and no threat cues, the reduced positive trait generalization could simply reflect the direct application of learned stereotypes.
To address this potential confound, in Study 2b, we manipulated social status without any trait-related behavioral descriptions.
This way, we were able to isolate the relationship between status-based stereotypes and positive trait coherence.

text.text: Study 2b.
Stereotype endorsement predicts positive trait coherence after learning about social status.
Participants read a passage describing two fictitious groups: the higherstatus Bwisi and the lower-status Mwangai, without attributing any traits or behaviors to either group.
Participants then rated the warmth and competence of 16 white male faces, eight labeled as members of each group, each shown at three levels of agency-or communion-related appearance (Figure 5a).
text.formatted: Participants then rated the warmth and competence of 16 white male faces, eight labeled as members of each group, each shown at three levels of agency-or communion-related appearance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5a</ref>).

text.text: We indexed trait coherence in two ways: the correlation between warmth and competence ratings across identities (identity-based coherence) and the extent to which warmth-related appearance raised competence ratings and vice versa (transfer slopes).
Participants rated each group's overall warmth and competence, allowing us to calculate the competence stereotype gap between the two groups.
We first tested whether ratings differed across the three manipulation levels and between the two groups.
This particular analysis was not preregistered.

Overall, members of the advantaged group received higher competence ratings (F(1, 301) = 62.90, p < .001, ηp² = 0.17, 95% CI [0.11, 0.24]) and warmth ratings (F(1, 301) = 7.10, p = .008, ηp² = 0.02, 95% CI [0.00, 0.06]) than members of the disadvantaged group.

text.text: For the warmth-to-competence transfer block, ratings increased across the three stimulus levels; for the competence-to-warmth transfer block, however, ratings were higher for the original faces than for both manipulated levels, resulting in a non-monotonic pattern across stimulus levels (Figure 5b).

text.text: These patterns supported the use of two complementary indices that separately captured identity-based coherence and manipulation-based transfer.
Detailed pairwise comparisons are reported in the Supplementary Information Section 3.
As preregistered, we examined group differences in coherence and cross-trait transfer after introducing participants to two novel groups.
We then tested whether stereotype endorsement predicted the gaps in coherence and transfer between the advantaged and disadvantaged groups, via one-tailed tests.

We did not observe group differences in any of the three indices: identity-based coherence, t(285) = -0.47, p = .681, Cohen's |d| = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.09]; warmth-to-competence transfer slope, t(301) = -0.07, p = .528, Cohen's |d| < 0.01, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.11]; or competence-to-warmth transfer slope, t(301) = -0.40, p = .654, Cohen's |d| = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.09].

text.text: Our preregistered primary stereotype index, defined as the difference in competence stereotype ratings between the advantaged and disadvantaged groups, predicted the identitybased coherence gap (β = 0.13, 95% CI [0.01, 0.24], p = .016) and the warmth-to-competence transfer gap (β = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = .039), but not the competence-to-warmth transfer gap (β = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.05], p = .851), as shown in Figure 5c.
text.formatted: Our preregistered primary stereotype index, defined as the difference in competence stereotype ratings between the advantaged and disadvantaged groups, predicted the identitybased coherence gap (β = 0.13, 95% CI [0.01, 0.24], p = .016) and the warmth-to-competence transfer gap (β = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = .039), but not the competence-to-warmth transfer gap (β = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.05], p = .851), as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5c</ref>.

text.text: However, the preregistered secondary stereotype index, a composite stereotype index combining the competence difference favoring the advantaged group with the warmth difference favoring the disadvantaged group did not significantly predict the coherence or transfer gaps: identity-based coherence gap, β = 0.00, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.12], p = .496; warmth-to-competence transfer gap, β = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.15], p = .290; or competence-to-warmth transfer gap, β = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.10], p = .582.
This may be because participants varied substantially in their warmth stereotypes.
Some participants showed a compensatory pattern, assigning relatively higher warmth to the disadvantaged group, whereas others rated the advantaged group higher on both competence and warmth.
Consequently, the warmth stereotype gap may not have captured between-group differences in stereotype endorsement consistently across participants.

To summarize, after learning about the social status of the novel groups, participants who showed a larger competence stereotype gap between the two groups also showed a larger group difference in identity-based warmth-competence coherence and in the positive influence of facial warmth on competence judgments.

These findings suggest that spontaneously formed stereotypes following exposure to social status information may contribute to differences in positive trait coherence, even in the absence of explicit stereotype information.
This pattern is consistent with the findings from our observations in Study 1.
These findings reveal trait coherence-the tendency for positive qualities to cohere in impression formation (Rosenberg et al., 1968)-as a previously overlooked source of bias in social perception.

text.text: Whereas classic accounts of Implicit Personality Theory and the halo effect posit that favorable traits are positively associated and readily generalize across dimensions (Schneider, 1973), across four correlational datasets and two experiments, spanning established and novel social groups, we show that this tendency depends on targets' group status in combination with perceivers' stereotype endorsement.
text.formatted: Whereas classic accounts of Implicit Personality Theory and the halo effect posit that favorable traits are positively associated and readily generalize across dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Schneider, 1973)</ref>, across four correlational datasets and two experiments, spanning established and novel social groups, we show that this tendency depends on targets' group status in combination with perceivers' stereotype endorsement.

text.text: Among highly stereotype-endorsing perceivers, advantaged groups showed stronger coherence between positive traits than disadvantaged groups.
Stereotypes therefore do more than introduce negative content into social judgments: they can alter how positive information is integrated across traits.
Notably, learning about group status alone did not produce a coherence gap for novel groups (Study 2b).
Instead, the gap grew with the competence stereotype participants formed, suggesting that stereotype endorsement, rather than status information per se, is key.

Although facial impression research has emphasized a common structure organized around fundamental dimensions of social evaluation (Jones et al., 2021; Todorov et al., 2008), growing evidence indicates that this structure is more flexible than previously assumed, varying across perceivers, cultures, and social contexts (Hong & Freeman, 2024; Oh et al., 2020 Oh et al., , 2022;; Stolier et al., 2018 Stolier et al., , 2020;; Xie et al., 2021).

text.text: Our findings are consistent with recent evidence that group membership shapes the structure of facial impressions.
For example, facial impression structures have been shown to differ across ingroup and outgroup targets in the association between trustworthiness and dominance (Hong & Freeman, 2024).
text.formatted: For example, facial impression structures have been shown to differ across ingroup and outgroup targets in the association between trustworthiness and dominance <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hong & Freeman, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our results identify a further form of group differentiation: among highly stereotype-endorsing perceivers, desirable traits were less coherent for disadvantaged than advantaged groups.
Although these group distinctions differ, both point to a role for social categorization in shaping trait inference.

Self-Categorization Theory proposes that stereotyping is rooted in the categorization of oneself and others into social groups; salient group categorizations accentuate perceived similarities among members within a category and differences between categories along relevant dimensions (Haslam et al., 1992; Haslam & Turner, 1992).
text.formatted: Self-Categorization Theory proposes that stereotyping is rooted in the categorization of oneself and others into social groups; salient group categorizations accentuate perceived similarities among members within a category and differences between categories along relevant dimensions <ref type="bibr">(Haslam et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haslam & Turner, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this framework by showing that social categorization can shape trait coherence across different forms of group differentiation, including distinctions based on social advantage and disadvantage.

These findings may initially appear to sit in tension with the minority-group homogeneity effect, whereby minority-group members are perceived as more similar to one another than majority-group members (Tepper & Gilovich, 2025).
text.formatted: These findings may initially appear to sit in tension with the minority-group homogeneity effect, whereby minority-group members are perceived as more similar to one another than majority-group members <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Tepper & Gilovich, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, our results may simply reflect a related process operating at a different level of representation.

The Continuum Model of impression formation proposes that perceivers shift between category-based processing, which treats group members as interchangeable instances of a category, and individuating processing, which attends to each person's unique configuration of attributes (Fiske & Neuberg, 1990).
text.formatted: The Continuum Model of impression formation proposes that perceivers shift between category-based processing, which treats group members as interchangeable instances of a category, and individuating processing, which attends to each person's unique configuration of attributes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fiske & Neuberg, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: If positive trait coherence reflects the integration of trait information within individual impressions (Rosenberg et al., 1968; Thorndike, 1920), category-based processing may weaken this integration for disadvantaged-group members, whereas individuation may preserve stronger coherence for advantaged-group members.
text.formatted: If positive trait coherence reflects the integration of trait information within individual impressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rosenberg et al., 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Thorndike, 1920)</ref>, category-based processing may weaken this integration for disadvantaged-group members, whereas individuation may preserve stronger coherence for advantaged-group members.

text.text: Consistent with this account, trustworthiness and dominance are more positively associated for ingroup than outgroup faces (Hong & Freeman, 2024), paralleling the asymmetry we observe between advantaged and disadvantaged groups.
text.formatted: Consistent with this account, trustworthiness and dominance are more positively associated for ingroup than outgroup faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hong & Freeman, 2024)</ref>, paralleling the asymmetry we observe between advantaged and disadvantaged groups.

text.text: Whether category-based processing contributes to this coherence gap remains an important question for future research.

Although the present studies do not directly examine the mechanisms linking stereotype endorsement to trait coherence, one possible explanation concerns the different social meanings of warmth and competence.

Competence is often closely tied to objective status relations and is therefore more readily confirmed (Cuddy et al., 2009; Fiske, 1993), whereas warmth is less closely linked to objective indicators, making its perceptions more ambiguous (Tausch et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Competence is often closely tied to objective status relations and is therefore more readily confirmed <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cuddy et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fiske, 1993)</ref>, whereas warmth is less closely linked to objective indicators, making its perceptions more ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Tausch et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This asymmetry may give advantaged groups greater latitude to be perceived as both competent and warm (Oldmeadow & Fiske, 2010), allowing positive information in one domain to generalize more readily to the other.
text.formatted: This asymmetry may give advantaged groups greater latitude to be perceived as both competent and warm <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Oldmeadow & Fiske, 2010)</ref>, allowing positive information in one domain to generalize more readily to the other.

text.text: For disadvantaged groups, stereotypes that associate warmth with lower competence may instead constrain such cross-trait generalization, weakening the positive coherence otherwise observed in person perception.
A second possibility is that weaker coherence reflects backlash against stereotype-incongruent impressions.
The Status Incongruity Hypothesis proposes that people who violate culturally prescribed expectations can face penalties that reinforce existing status hierarchies (Rudman et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The Status Incongruity Hypothesis proposes that people who violate culturally prescribed expectations can face penalties that reinforce existing status hierarchies <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Rudman et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Positive impressions of disadvantaged group members may similarly be constrained when they conflict with stereotype-based expectations, limiting their generalization across traits.

More broadly, these findings may be understood within a high-dimensional view of social perception, in which traits and social categories are embedded in an intercorrelated space of social knowledge (Freeman & Lin, 2025).
text.formatted: More broadly, these findings may be understood within a high-dimensional view of social perception, in which traits and social categories are embedded in an intercorrelated space of social knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Freeman & Lin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Within such a space, conceptual associations can propagate across related features, allowing initial inferences to shape broader impressions.
Our findings extend this account by showing that stereotype-related group information is associated with systematic differences in the coherence among positive traits.

Group-trait associations and trait-trait associations could therefore be represented within the same structure, such that activating a group concept changes the associations through which subsequent trait information is interpreted.

From this perspective, advantaged groups may function as relatively unmarked or "default" social categories, whereas disadvantaged groups may carry additional stereotype-based associations (Bailey et al., 2019; Stroessner, 1996; Zárate & Smith, 1990).
text.formatted: From this perspective, advantaged groups may function as relatively unmarked or "default" social categories, whereas disadvantaged groups may carry additional stereotype-based associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bailey et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Stroessner, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Zárate & Smith, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: For a perceiver who strongly endorses these stereotypes, activating a disadvantaged group concept may therefore introduce additional associations into the trait network, competing with the positive associations that ordinarily support halo-like generalization.
The findings also suggest how stereotypes can produce discrimination without requiring overt negative evaluations.
Most contemporary discrimination operates less through explicit hostility toward disadvantaged groups than through favoritism toward advantaged ones (Greenwald & Pettigrew, 2014).
text.formatted: Most contemporary discrimination operates less through explicit hostility toward disadvantaged groups than through favoritism toward advantaged ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Greenwald & Pettigrew, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Stronger cross-trait generalization for advantaged groups offers one cognitive route for such favoritism.
Advantaged group members may benefit when evidence of one desirable quality supports inferences about others, whereas disadvantaged group members may need to establish each quality independently.

This extends work on shifting and double standards, which shows that members of devalued groups must provide more evidence to be judged as possessing a given ability (Biernat & Kobrynowicz, 1997; Foschi, 2000).
text.formatted: This extends work on shifting and double standards, which shows that members of devalued groups must provide more evidence to be judged as possessing a given ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Biernat & Kobrynowicz, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Foschi, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that a similar burden may operate across traits.
This kind of asymmetry could matter wherever impressions accumulate across multiple judgments, as in hiring, promotion, networking, and recommendation decisions.
Small evaluative differences can compound into substantial disparities (Martell et al., 1996), particularly when a candidate's qualifications are ambiguous (Dovidio & Gaertner, 2000).
text.formatted: Small evaluative differences can compound into substantial disparities <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Martell et al., 1996)</ref>, particularly when a candidate's qualifications are ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dovidio & Gaertner, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Several constraints limit our conclusions.
First, although our samples included participants from the U.S. and Singapore, the cultural range remains limited, and it is unclear whether the same pattern extends to other cultures.
Second, the present studies do not directly distinguish among the mechanisms linking stereotype endorsement to trait coherence.

Stereotype-endorsing perceivers may actively apply group-specific expectations during impression formation, or repeated exposure to stereotype-based associations may gradually alter the links among traits.
We also did not measure prejudice directly, leaving unclear whether the observed coherence fragmentation reflects prejudiced attitudes per se or familiarity with culturally shared stereotypes.

This distinction is relevant to the Stereotype Content Model, which links patterns of warmth and competence to differentiated forms of emotional prejudice (Caprariello et al., 2009; Fiske et al., 2002).
text.formatted: This distinction is relevant to the Stereotype Content Model, which links patterns of warmth and competence to differentiated forms of emotional prejudice <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caprariello et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fiske et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our studies rely on face-based impressions or conceptual inferences about briefly described, unfamiliar group members, both of which provide limited individuating information.
For unfamiliar faces, salient social-category cues such as gender and age may increase reliance on category-based processing and amplify the influence of group stereotypes on trait structure.
Future work using richer representations of familiar individuals will help establish the boundary conditions and real-world magnitude of this effect.
This research demonstrates that stereotypes can fragment the positive coherence of social impressions.

Among stereotype-endorsing perceivers, positive evaluations of disadvantaged group members are less likely to generalize across traits, whereas advantaged group members benefit from stronger positive trait coherence.
This extends research on bias beyond the content of social evaluations to the way trait information is integrated during impression formation.
This fragmentation may require marginalized individuals to establish positive qualities independently while advantaged groups benefit from cross-trait amplification.

These findings suggest that an important consequence of stereotype-based bias is not only what perceivers infer about marginalized individuals, but also how readily one positive quality leads to the recognition of others.
